evidence: AddProductUseCase.ts: implements AddProduct, takes ProductRepository, uses Product.create(command) and toStockLevelDto; the only duplicate-ID check is the ConflictError throw.
ListCatalogueUseCase.ts and ListStockLevelsUseCase.ts: both map results through toCatalogueItemDto and toStockLevelDto from ProductMapper.ts.
CatalogueModule.ts: createCatalogueUseCases is the single wiring point and returns the CatalogueUseCases interface.
ProductDtos.ts: AddProductCommand, CatalogueItemDto and StockLevelDto are the single definition of the module's data shapes.
productCommandParsers.ts: parseAddProductCommand uses requireRecord, requireString and requireInteger from the shared inputGuards and returns AddProductCommand.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: All seven files serve one concern: the product catalogue and stock use cases. Each use case has an interface and an implementation and takes the ProductRepository abstraction. CatalogueModule is the only place that wires them together. DTOs live in ProductDtos.ts and the domain-to-DTO mapping lives in ProductMapper.ts. All three use cases go through that mapper, and none builds DTOs inline. Input parsing for AddProductCommand sits in productCommandParsers.ts and reuses the shared inputGuards. The duplicate-product check (ConflictError) appears only in AddProductUseCase. Product construction goes through Product.create, so domain invariants stay in the domain. The mapper reads some fields directly (product.id) and others from toSnapshot(). That is a minor stylistic difference, not a duplicated rule or a bypass of the module's abstractions.
